card.hook: Look up at Canton Tower and it seems to be holding its breath, pinching in at the middle like it's squeezing into a smaller size. Locals call it "Slim Waist", and once you see it, you can't unsee it.
card.stand_here: Stand near 艺苑路, at the phone icon on the map, about 170 m south-west of the tower. Face north-east and hold your phone upright.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the tower's full height in from this close. Switch to 1x for a less stretched look at the waist, then try 2x or 5x for the lattice and the top section (higher zooms depend on your phone).
card.make_it_pop: Tap the tower, then slide the brightness down a little so the sky doesn't wash out and the lattice stays crisp.
card.best_time: Late afternoon to dusk is lovely, because the sky colours contrast nicely with the tower's shape. It's probably lit up in the evening too, which gives night shots a whole different look.
card.selfie_here: Sit on the Huachenghui stairs by Opera House Metro Station Exit E, with the tower behind you, and use the front camera. At dusk, head to the middle of the pedestrian Haixin Bridge, face the tower and try a backlit selfie or a silhouette.
card.ask_someone: For a full-tower portrait, try the big open lawn in Ersha Island Art Park and ask someone to stand where the whole tower is in view while you pose on the lawn.
card.rules_and_safety: The area around the tower is public and you can walk there, but the tower's decks and attractions may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Tilt up, then step back a few paces and zoom in slightly instead, and see how much straighter the tower gets.
card.good_to_know: Canton Tower is a 600-metre observation tower in Haizhu District. It opened in September 2010, just before the Asian Games that Guangzhou hosted, and for a short while it was the tallest tower in the world. Dutch architects designed it with the engineering firm Arup, and the twist comes from rotating two ovals, one at the base and one near the top, against each other.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near 艺苑路, at the phone icon on the map, about 170 m south-west of the tower. Face north-east and hold your phone upright.

card.hook: One canal crossing and Guangzhou's honking streets go quiet. You're under big trees, with old verandahed mansions on both sides and bronze statues standing around like they're waiting for someone.
card.stand_here: Head to the phone icon on the map, near 沙面一街. It's about 290 m east of the subject, so stand there and face west.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for street scenes and building fronts. Go to zoom 0.5x to fit a whole tree-lined avenue in, then zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for verandahs, church fronts and statues.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up an avenue so the trees frame each side and the buildings lead the eye in, keeping your phone level so nothing leans.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon is usually nicest, because the light is softer and the island tends to be quieter. If the bright sky is washing out the buildings, tap the building and drag the slider to make it a bit darker.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the open ground in front of Our Lady of Lourdes Church on Shamian South Street, with the Gothic church behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x so the cream walls and Tiffany-blue window frames fit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand back from the zebra crossing in front of the Former HSBC Bank Building (No. 54 Shamian Main Street) while you stand in the middle of the crossing, so the big columned facade ends up behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The paving can be slippery when it's wet, and the Pearl River promenade is exposed to the weather, so shorten that stretch in ordinary rain and postpone the walk in thunderstorms or official weather warnings. The Former HSBC building's outside is fine to photograph, but its inside is closed to visitors, and other buildings, churches and hotels may have their own access rules.
card.challenge: Find a bronze statue, switch to portrait mode and get close for a shot of it alone. Then take a second one of you copying its pose.
card.good_to_know: Shamian Island is a small sandbank island of about 0.3 square kilometres, roughly 900 m east to west and 300 m north to south. In 1859 it was split between Britain and France, and the old trading mansions and churches are still there. Christ Church Shameen dates from 1865, and Our Lady of Lourdes Chapel, finished in 1892, stands at the French end.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to the phone icon on the map, near 沙面一街. It's about 290 m east of the subject, so stand there and face west.

card.hook: Try to find a straight line on this building. Go on, we'll wait. Zaha Hadid designed it as two rocks washed smooth by the Pearl River, so it looks like a pair of giant pebbles, and that makes it a great phone subject.
card.stand_here: Stand in the open square, 花城广场, with the opera house about 2 minutes on foot to the west. Face west and you'll see it in a row with the library and the museum, with the Canton Tower rising behind.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole row of buildings in. Then switch to 1x for a cleaner shot of the opera house alone, and try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for the Canton Tower or the stone details.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the opera house, then slide the brightness down a touch so the pale stone and sky keep their detail.
card.best_time: Late afternoon to dusk is lovely, because the light is softer on the stone. Early morning is likely to be quieter. After dark, use night mode and tuck your elbows into your body, or rest the phone on a ledge, to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Head to the mirrored pool on the North Gate steps (use the North Gate entrance, not the South Gate, which is for performance access), or to the front fountain. Both have the building reflected in the water, so hold your front camera at arm's length, try zoom 0.5x, and let the curves fill the space over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on the Pearl River side of the building to shoot back toward it, so the whole structure fits in the frame with you in front.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole square, then one close-up where the stone curves fill the frame, and see if your friends can tell they're the same building.
card.good_to_know: The opera house opened on 9 May 2010 and took over five years to build. The auditorium is concrete, set inside a granite and glass-clad steel frame. It's the biggest performing centre in southern China.

card.hook: Look up at the Gathering Hall roof and you'll find 224 tiny figures from traditional dramas lined up along a ceramic ridge, like a very small, very crowded theatre.
card.stand_here: Once you're inside the complex, walk to the stone platform in front of Juxian Hall (聚贤堂) and face the main hall. It's a separate spot you reach on foot, not something you see from the gate.
card.zoom: Use zoom 1x for the platform and its balustrade. Go to 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for the ridge figures and carved details. In the courtyards and lanes, switch to zoom 0.5x to fit the whole roofline or a tall wall in one frame.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the carved detail you want sharp, then drag the brightness down a little (darker) so the bright sky doesn't wash out the ceramic roof.
card.best_time: Go when the site opens, or later in the afternoon, when the light is softer and the courtyards are quieter. Check the official site for opening days before you go.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie on the terrace in front of Juxian Hall with the main hall behind you. Use the front camera, hold it a little low, and let the carved stone and iron railings frame you.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by and ask them to stand across the street from the three-arch gate while you stand in front of it, so you and the whole gate fit in one frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Flash is not allowed, drones aren't permitted, and please don't block the central doorways to pose. It's still a working ancestral hall, so keep clear of ceremonies and offerings. Some areas are dimly lit, so watch your step on the polished stone floors.
card.challenge: Find the flying-cod finials at the tips of the roof ridge and get them in the same frame as one of the little drama figures.
card.good_to_know: The hall was finished in 1894 with money from Chen families across Guangdong. It was built as an ancestral temple and a place to prepare young clansmen for the imperial exams. Today it houses the Guangdong Folk Art Museum, in a symmetrical complex of 19 buildings, nine halls and six courtyards. The showpiece ridge on the Gathering Hall roof stretches about 27 metres.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Once you're inside the complex, walk to the stone platform in front of Juxian Hall (聚贤堂) and face the main hall. It's a separate spot you reach on foot, not something you see from the gate.

card.hook: Picture a big pale stone statue glowing against dark green leaves, with a set of stone steps leading your eye straight up to it. That's the Five Rams at Yuexiu Park, and it's the first stop for a reason.
card.stand_here: Walk up to the Five Rams Sculpture (五羊石像) and stand on the stone steps beside it, facing the statue and looking up. Go up a few steps, then turn round to catch the steps and greenery in front for a bit of depth.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the statue, the steps and the trees in one shot. If you're close, tap 0.5x to get the whole sculpture and the greenery in the frame. If crowds are in the way, try 2x or more (it depends on your phone) to pick out the rams against the leaves.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the statue on a vertical line, then tap the statue and drag the slider to make the picture a little darker so the pale stone keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Morning gives you cleaner light and fewer people. Late afternoon is softer and warmer.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie on the stone steps directly below the Five Rams Sculpture, with the rams rising above you over your shoulder. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and let the trees around you add some dramatic light.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in Wuyang Stone Statue Square, in front of the Five Rams statue, and take your photo with the rams behind you, ideally in the morning for a full view of all five.
card.rules_and_safety: Paths inside the park can be steep in places, so wear comfortable shoes. Zhenhai Tower and Guangzhou Museum may charge entry and close on certain days, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Frame the statue with a few branches in the top corners and the steps along the bottom, then see if you can count all five rams in your photo.
card.good_to_know: The Five Rams Sculpture was finished in 1960 from more than 130 pieces of granite. It stands for the five rams of local legend that gave Guangzhou the nickname "City of Rams", and many locals see them as lucky. If you have time, Zhenhai Tower on the hill was first built as a guard tower in 1380 and has housed the Guangzhou Museum since 1928.

card.hook: Hold your phone low in the courtyard, tilt it up, and a 57-metre pagoda climbs out of the bottom of your screen with banyan branches hanging in at the edges. It's a tall, layered shot, and you never have to leave the courtyard.
card.stand_here: From 87 Liurong Road, the middle of the temple grounds is about 1 minute on foot to the south-west. Stand in the courtyard right at the front of the Flower Pagoda and face it, with the phone tilted up.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x so the whole pagoda and the trees fit. If you can step back, zoom 1x gives a more natural shape. Then try zoom 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) for the layered roof edges and the colourful details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the pagoda up with a vertical line, then tap the pagoda and slide it a little darker so the sky stays blue.
card.best_time: Go in the morning, when the sun shows off the pagoda's colours. One guide suggests about 8:00 to 10:00, when the courtyard is quieter. In summer (roughly June to mid-July) the lotus pond also looks pretty, best in the morning.
card.selfie_here: Head to Flower Pagoda Square, the courtyard at the base of the Flower Pagoda, and stand with the tower directly behind you. Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x and hold it a bit low so the pagoda rises over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by and ask them to step well back across the pagoda courtyard while you stand in front of the pagoda.
card.rules_and_safety: No flash, and no photos of the Buddha statues inside the halls. Outdoor courtyard shots are fine. Photography can be restricted during worship, so don't photograph worshippers up close without asking, and keep your voice low.
card.challenge: Get the whole pagoda in one shot with branches on both edges and the tower lined up on a gridline, then see if you can do it without a single stranger's head in the frame.
card.good_to_know: The temple was first built in AD 537, and the pagoda dates from 1097. It was rebuilt in 1373 after a fire and restored in 1900, though the exact ages are approximate. The name comes from a poem called "Six Banyans", written by Su Shi after a visit.

card.hook: From outside, the Guangdong Museum looks like a bold, angular box that someone set down on a big grassy slope. Inside that shape is the idea of a Cantonese ivory puzzle ball, with layers nested inside layers.
card.stand_here: Stand on 花城广场 (Huacheng Square), on the west side of the museum. The museum is to the east of you, so face east, and the facade lines up with Canton Tower and the East and West Towers behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the museum, Canton Tower and the two towers into one frame. Then switch to 1x for a cleaner, less stretched view of the facade. If your phone has 2x to 5x, use it for a tighter shot of the museum's angles with the towers behind.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the museum on one side and let Canton Tower rise in the gap beside it, keeping the phone level so the building's edges stay straight.
card.best_time: No best time is confirmed for this view, so go when the light suits you. Soft light earlier or later in the day is kinder to the facade than harsh midday sun, and if you stay into the evening, try night mode with your phone braced against something solid.
card.selfie_here: Use the same spot on the west side of 花城广场. Switch to the front camera (try 0.5x if your phone has it), face away from the museum and let the building and Canton Tower sit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the west side of the square and frame the museum with you in front, so the building, Canton Tower and the East and West Towers all fit.
card.rules_and_safety: Visitor guides say selfie sticks are banned inside the museum, so leave yours in your bag if you go in. The guides don't list a rule for the outdoor square.
card.challenge: Take three shots of the facade (far, middle, close) and see which one looks most like a puzzle ball to you.
card.good_to_know: The museum opened in May 2010 in Zhujiang New Town, replacing the older museum on Wenming Road. It's the province's general museum of art, nature, culture and history. Entry to the galleries may need an advance booking, so check the official site before you go.

card.hook: Picture a plain white tower with no decoration at all, standing out against the Guangzhou sky. For centuries it was the tallest thing in the city, and it's still a showstopper.
card.stand_here: Stand on 光塔路 (Guangta Road) in front of the main gate at No. 56, facing the minaret. You'll get the gate with the white tower rising beside it, the classic postcard view.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the gate and minaret together in one upright shot. If you're tight against the gate, tap 0.5x. Then try 2x to 5x for the top of the tower or the roof eaves.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the white minaret, then slide the brightness a little darker so the pale surface keeps its detail against the bright sky.
card.best_time: Go in the daytime, when the gate is open, and skip Friday around noon, when access is restricted for prayers. Early morning or late afternoon is often calmer on the street.
card.selfie_here: Pose on the pavement on Guangta Road in front of the red-brick main gate with the green awning, so the minaret rises beside and behind you. Use the front camera, and if your phone has a 0.5x button on it, it helps fit the tower in over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the opposite side of Guangta Road from the gate while you pose at the gate, so the minaret is framed above the street wall.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a working mosque, so keep a low profile. Photos are fine outside and in the courtyard, but not inside the prayer hall. Keep your flash off and ask before photographing any worshippers.
card.challenge: Keep the tower perfectly straight. Hold your phone upright, line the minaret up with a gridline, and don't tilt up, or it will lean like it's had a long day.
card.good_to_know: Huaisheng Mosque is the main mosque of Guangzhou, also known as the Lighthouse Mosque. The minaret is about 36 metres tall and was the city's tallest building until the early 20th century. In the Middle Ages it worked as a lighthouse for river traffic as well as a wind vane. The mosque was rebuilt in 1350 and again in 1695 after a fire.

card.hook: Old arcade columns on one side, a granite Gothic tower on the other: Guangzhou doesn't do subtle. Locals call this place the Stone House, and once you see the street view you'll get why.
card.stand_here: Stand on Yide Road (一德路) on the arcade side, then turn and look back to the north-east towards Sacred Heart Cathedral. Let the old arcade buildings sit in the foreground.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so you get the arcade and the cathedral together. Try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to bring the towers closer, and keep 0.5x for when you want lots of arcade, because it makes the towers look smaller and can make them lean.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the cathedral on the screen, then drag the slider to make the picture a little darker so the pale granite and sky don't turn white.
card.best_time: Soft daylight suits the pale granite best. The cathedral is closed on some days, so check the schedule before you head over.
card.selfie_here: Use the front plaza outside the main gate with the façade and twin towers right behind you. Hold the front camera a bit low so both towers fit over your shoulder. If you'd rather dodge the crowds, the red stone steps at the side entrance are said to be quieter, though the exact spot is hard to pin down.
card.ask_someone: Ask your helper to stand on the front plaza, well back from the gate and centred on the main entrance, while you stand a little way in front of the gate, clear of it, so the whole façade, rose window and both towers fit in.
card.rules_and_safety: The cathedral is a working place of worship. Inside, photos are fine but no flash and no selfie sticks, and no photos or wandering around during Mass. It's reportedly closed on Mondays and possibly the third Sunday of each month, so check the official site first.
card.challenge: Turn on your gridlines and see if you can keep the arcade columns and both tower walls perfectly straight in one shot.
card.good_to_know: Almost everything here is granite, including the walls, pillars and both towers, which is unusual for a cathedral anywhere. The twin towers rise about 53 metres, and the building was finished in 1888 after 25 years of work, much of it done by hand. The site was once the home of the Qing viceroy, and the façade was modelled on a church in Paris.

card.hook: Here's the problem with a 438.6 m glass skyscraper: it won't fit in your phone screen, however far back you wobble. So don't try to catch all of it. Go for a bold, simple shot instead.
card.stand_here: Stand in Huacheng Square, at the northern end of the square. Face the Guangzhou International Finance Center, and you can get the IFC West Tower, the CTF East Tower and the Canton Tower framed together in one shot.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x, because you're close to a very tall building. Switch to 1x for a tighter, less stretched view of the lower floors. Try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the glass pattern near the top.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the tower's edge up with a vertical line, then tap the sky or the brightest part of the glass and slide the brightness down a touch so the sky stays blue.
card.best_time: Late afternoon or just after sunset is usually the most atmospheric, while the sky still has some colour. On clear days, a morning visit can give you a clean blue sky. After dark, use night mode and tuck your elbows into your body to keep the phone steady.
card.selfie_here: Head to the eastern plaza of Huacheng Square and stand with the IFC rising behind you, so the building fills your background. Use the front camera, hold it low and slightly above you, and let the tower tower over your shoulder. For a different look, try the irregular steps of the Guangzhou Opera House on the west side of the square, with the towers behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the open plaza in front of the IFC and shoot upward, while you stand at the bottom of the frame with the skyscrapers towering above you.
card.rules_and_safety: Watch your belongings at night and be careful of pickpockets.
card.challenge: Find a tree or a friendly stranger, put them at the edge of your frame, and see if you can make the tower look even taller.
card.good_to_know: The tower has 103 storeys, was completed in 2010, and was designed by WilkinsonEyre. It won the RIBA Lubetkin Prize in 2012. Inside are offices, a Four Seasons hotel and an observation deck on floors 99 and 100, and as of 2023 it was the world's tallest building with a rooftop helipad.

card.hook: Picture red walls, grey-green tiled roofs and big shady trees, all so calm you'll find yourself lowering your voice. That's the courtyard at Guangxiao Temple, and the Mahavira Hall fills your phone screen without any effort.
card.stand_here: Stand in the courtyard directly in front of the Mahavira Hall, on its central axis, and face the hall straight on. The red walls and tiled roof fill the frame, with the flowering trees around them.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the straight-on view. If the roofline won't fit, tap 0.5x. Save 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for roof tiles, carved windows and the tops of the pagodas.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, line the middle of the hall up with the centre of the screen, and keep the phone level so the pillars don't lean.
card.best_time: Come in roughly February to March, when the yellow blossom adds colour in front of the hall. Outside flower season, a quieter time of day gives you cleaner frames with fewer people in front of the hall.
card.selfie_here: Stand beside the seven-storey Hair-Burying Pagoda on the flat courtyard floor. It sits among trees and yellow cloths, so it makes a nice landmark behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to squeeze more in, and keep the pagoda over your shoulder. For a quieter backdrop, the bamboo path just behind the West Iron Pagoda in the garden area is said to have almost no crowds.
card.ask_someone: Stand on the open ground in front of the Mahavira Hall and ask a passer-by to shoot straight on, so the red walls and roof fill the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Don't photograph the Buddha statues, and photography is prohibited inside the Sixth Patriarch Hall. No flash in the halls, and please respect any No Photos signs. Shoot the buildings, courtyards and pagodas from outside. This is an active temple and may be ticketed, so check the official site for current entry arrangements.
card.challenge: Get the hall perfectly symmetrical, with the red walls straight and the blossom framing both sides, then see if a friend can spot which tree you used.
card.good_to_know: The temple was first built in 401 and last rebuilt in 1654, and it took its present name in 1482. In front of the hall stands the Great Compassion Column from 826. Behind it are two small iron pagodas from the 960s, said to be the oldest iron towers in China.

card.hook: Picture a building crew in 1983, digging in the middle of Guangzhou, and bumping into a king's tomb. That's how this place began, and it makes a great story to tell with your photos.
card.stand_here: Head to the phone icon on the map, which sits in the middle of the museum site on Elephant Hill at 867 Jiefang Road. Turn slowly on the spot and frame the museum buildings around you, instead of hunting for one perfect view.
card.zoom: Use 1x for most outdoor shots. Go to 0.5x when you want the full width of a building or the forecourt, and 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for details and objects in display cases.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines and line up the building edges with them so the walls stay straight, then step back to fit in some sky.
card.best_time: A bright but hazy or lightly overcast day gives soft, flattering light on the buildings. Early on a weekday morning usually means fewer people in your shots. Check the official site for opening times before you go.
card.selfie_here: Find the stone lions by the main entrance and stand with the building behind you. Hold your front camera at arm's length, and guides say the lit lions look especially striking at night.
card.ask_someone: Stand in front of the glass pyramid above the tomb, on the Tomb Exhibition Area side, and ask someone to shoot upward at 0.5x so the pyramid rises behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Flash is prohibited, especially in exhibition halls and tomb chambers, and photography isn't allowed in some lower levels of the tomb chambers. Ceilings are low in some tomb areas, so keep a close eye on children. Check on arrival whether the tomb itself is open.
card.challenge: Find the strongest shape in the museum, a bronze or a piece of jade, and fill the whole frame with just that one object.
card.good_to_know: The tomb belongs to Zhao Mo, who ruled the Nanyue kingdom from 137 BC to 122 BC. It lies about 20 metres underground, is built from 750 large stones, and its seven chambers held more than 1,000 burial objects. The star is a jade garment sewn together with silk thread.

card.hook: Picture a huge blue-roofed octagon sitting calmly on green lawns, right in the middle of busy Guangzhou. The Sun Yat-sen Memorial Hall is hard to miss, and it's even harder to take a bad photo of it.
card.stand_here: Stand about 590 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east towards the Sun Yat-sen Memorial Hall. Once you're in the grounds, you can wander closer for the other views.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the whole octagonal facade from the main square. Then try 0.5x to look up at the eaves with the tree branches around them. Finally, zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out roof edges and tile detail.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the roof or the sky-lit part of the building, then drag the slider a little darker so the sky doesn't wash out and the blue roof stays rich.
card.best_time: Spring is the best season, because one guide says the kapok trees flower then. Check the trees are actually there when you visit, as this tip comes from a single guide.
card.selfie_here: Head to the memorial square just inside the main gate and stand to the side of the bronze Sun Yat-sen statue, so the hall's facade stays behind you in the frame. For something quieter, go to the northeast corner under the kapok trees, where the branches and roof eaves make a classical backdrop. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the hall over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the square facing the main entrance, so the whole facade and the bronze statue fit in the frame, while you stand beside the statue.
card.rules_and_safety: Entering the building is ticketed, and indoor photography is limited to designated areas, so check the official site and the signs before you go in. The grounds can be photographed from outside.
card.challenge: Find the spot where the kapok branches and curved eaves overlap, and get the blue roof peeking through the branches.
card.good_to_know: Lu Yanzhi designed the hall, and it was built between 1929 and 1931 with donations from local and overseas Chinese people. It spans 71 metres with no pillars inside and seats 3,240 people. It stands on the site of the old Presidential Palace.

card.hook: Picture a deep red, five-tier tower rising out of the green treetops of Yuexiu Park, with roofs that sweep up like they're waving at you. It's been the star of Guangzhou's skyline since 1380, and it still knows how to pose.
card.stand_here: Head for Zhenhai Tower inside Yuexiu Park and stand on the open forecourt in front of the main entrance, where the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Face the tower and step back until the whole red building fits, with green trees on both sides.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the whole tower fits with some trees around it. If you're close to the steps, try 0.5x, but keep the phone level so the walls don't lean. Then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the roof corners and red walls.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the tower's walls up with the vertical lines, then tap the red wall and drag the brightness down a touch if the sky looks washed out.
card.best_time: One guide suggests coming around 16:00. People wander through the forecourt, so wait a moment for a gap and you'll get a clean shot.
card.selfie_here: Stand centred on the stone steps in front of the tower, so the red wall and green-tiled roof fill the background behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the tower over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a friendly passer-by to step back until the whole five-storey tower fits in the frame; one guide suggests the ridge road behind the tower for this, but check the exact spot on the map first.
card.rules_and_safety: One guide says photography is unrestricted in the park, but flash may be restricted inside the museum. One guide notes the tower is closed on Mondays, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take three shots from three different distances, then pick the one where the tower looks properly straight and tall.
card.good_to_know: Zhenhai Tower, also called the Five-Story Pagoda, was first built in 1380, at the start of the Ming dynasty. It's about 28 metres high, and when it went up it was the tallest building in the city. For a long time it was Guangzhou's symbol, until the Five Goats Statue took over, and today it houses the Guangzhou Museum.

card.hook: Five carved sheep are staring down at you from the entrance archway, and they have the best spot in old Guangzhou. Give them a nod, then get your phone out.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the phone icon on the map, at the archway at the entrance in front of the main hall. Face the archway so the five sheep sit in the middle, with the green-tiled gate and red walls around them.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the archway. If the courtyard is too tight to fit the gate and walls, tap 0.5x. Save 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the rear-hall roof and the footprint.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, tap the archway, then slide it a little darker so the sky and pale stonework don't wash out.
card.best_time: Go in the morning, before about 10:00, when the light comes from the east and suits the gate. Midday is busier at the archway and rear hall.
card.selfie_here: Take it at the stone archway at the entrance of the main hall. Use the front camera (0.5x if your phone has it) and let the five sheep sit over your shoulder. For a second one, find the footprint recess in the red sandstone on the east side of the rear hall. It's easy to miss, so ask at the gate or look in the eastern courtyard.
card.rules_and_safety: Check the official site before you go for opening days and entry rules. Don't photograph people who are praying in the main worship halls. If you climb the bell tower, the stairs are steep and not very wide.
card.challenge: Get all five sheep in one frame with the green gate behind them, then go and find the giant footprint and see whether a turtle has beaten you to it.
card.good_to_know: Legend says five immortals rode in on five coloured sheep carrying five grains, and the sheep turned to stone when the immortals left. That's why Guangzhou is called the City of the Rams. The present temple dates from 1377 or 1378, under the Ming. Its big bell, about 3 metres high and 5 tonnes, is called the Forbidden Bell because it hasn't been rung since a plague broke out.

card.hook: Five stone rams, a patch of sky and a ceiling of leaves: the trick here is looking up. Climb to the steps and the rams suddenly look huge.
card.stand_here: Stand on the stone steps right below the Five Rams Statue, where the phone icon sits on the map. Face the statue and aim up at the rams, with sky and tree canopy behind them.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x and tilt the phone upward. Try zoom 0.5x to fit in more leaves and sky, and keep the phone level so the edges don't stretch. For the side view, zoom 2x or more (depending on your phone) lets you pick out the rams without moving closer.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the rams on an upper crossing point, tap the rams, then slide the picture a little darker if the sky turns white.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning, before the crowds build up, for the best chance of clear steps. One guide says the light turns soft after 4 PM, so late afternoon is a good second option.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie on the stone steps beside the statue, where the trees shape the light. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and tuck the rams in over your shoulder. The square in front of the statue is another good spot, ideally in morning light.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the steps lower than the statue and shoot upward, then check that the rams made it into the frame with you.
card.rules_and_safety: The statue is free to reach inside the park, but check the official site for current park opening times and entry rules. People often pass on the steps, so keep your phone steady against your body.
card.challenge: Take three shots at different heights. Crouch a little lower each time and see how much taller the plinth and rams grow.
card.good_to_know: The Five Rams Statue is a stone sculpture of five rams on a plinth, on a hill inside Yuexiu Park. The park runs along Jiefang North Road. One tourism guide calls the rams the city's emblem, which makes this the classic Guangzhou photo.

card.hook: Picture the road tipping gently up in front of you, with heavy iron ribs and the river waiting at the far end. That's the Haizhu Bridge approach, and it practically draws the photo for you.
card.stand_here: Stand in 海珠广场 (Haizhu Square), on the slope at the north end that leads up to the bridge. The bridge lies to the south-east of this point, so face south along the ramp.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the ramp, the bridge and the river in one shot. When the kapok trees are in bloom, switch to 0.5x and let the branches arch across the top. Try zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the ironwork.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the bridge, then drag the slider to make it a little darker so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Come when the kapok trees are in bloom for the classic frame. The rest of the year, sunrise or blue hour suits the bridge best, especially from the south bank when it's lit.
card.selfie_here: Try the slope on the Guangzhou Hotel side, where the kapok trees line the approach. A guide calls it the best photo spot in the area, though not for selfies specifically. Use the front camera, or 0.5x to fit more in, with the bridge and blossom behind your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: For a second shot, go to the south bank near the bridge foot and ask a passer-by to take your photo while you stand with the bridge behind you, ideally at blue hour.
card.rules_and_safety: The bridge carries road traffic, so keep to the pavement and wait for a gap if you want a clean ramp. One guide says the river walk around the bridge is well lit and feels safe after dark.
card.challenge: Line the ramp's edge up with a gridline and catch it with no cars in the frame. Patience is the real skill here.
card.good_to_know: Haizhu Bridge was the first bridge ever built across the Pearl River in Guangzhou. Work ran from 1929 to 1933, and the American contractor Markton Company finished it. It was damaged in 1938 and again in 1949, and it still carries a two-lane road today.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in 海珠广场 (Haizhu Square), on the slope at the north end that leads up to the bridge. The bridge lies to the south-east of this point, so face south along the ramp.

card.hook: Picture a bright red wall, a huge kapok tree leaning over it, and sunshine pouring through the branches. That's the first thing you meet here, and you haven't even gone inside yet.
card.stand_here: Stand right in front of the main gate, 棂星门, and look up. Tilt your phone so the kapok branches fill the top of the picture and the red wall runs down one side.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the gate and the red wall. Switch to 0.5x if you want the whole canopy and wall in one go while you look up. For close-ups of flowers against the sky, try 2x to 5x, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the wall's straight edge with a grid line so it doesn't lean, then tap the red wall or the flowers and slide the picture a little darker so the bright sky doesn't wash out the colours.
card.best_time: Kapok flowers only bloom for a short time, roughly March to April, so that's when you'll get the best shots. Mornings from 10:00 to 12:00 or afternoons from 15:00 to 17:00 have the best light, according to photo guides. Outside those weeks, expect a plainer but still pleasant red-wall view.
card.selfie_here: Stand against the red wall by the main gate, use the front camera, and angle the phone upward so the kapok trees sit above you. For a second, more painterly selfie, walk straight in from the entrance to the eaves of Guangji Hall on the right side and stand between them, looking up toward the kapok. Try 0.5x if your phone has it.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the paved forecourt facing the main gate, so the entrance and hall roofs are behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Take photos freely outdoors, but obey any signs inside the halls. It's a museum site, so check the official site for opening days and times before you go.
card.challenge: Find the spot where the kapok branches and the red wall make a perfectly straight line, then get a portrait with the blossoms floating above your head.
card.good_to_know: This museum sits in a former Confucian temple first built in the 14th century. The institute opened on 3 July 1924 and trained young activists to take political ideas out to the countryside. Mao Zedong directed its sixth and largest class.
